spot.intro: Most sentences tell us **who or what** (the subject) and **what happens** (the verb). Many also say **who or what receives the action** (the object).

examples.note: Subject, verb and object.
Some sentences have no object.
Ask “who?” for the subject, then “what did they do?” for the verb.

try.q: Tap the subject.
try.text: Our neighbor bakes bread every morning.
try.why: The subject is who bakes: “Our neighbor” (or just “neighbor”).

try.q: Tap the verb.
try.text: The children play football after school.
try.why: The verb is the action: “play”.

try.q: Tap the object.
try.text: Sara bought a new phone yesterday.
try.why: The object is what Sara bought: “a new phone”. “Yesterday” tells us when.

try.q: Which word is the verb? “My cousin lives in a small town.”
try.why: “Lives” is the verb. “My cousin” is the subject.

try.q: Does each sentence have an object?
try.why: An object answers “what?” after the verb: the newspaper, dinner. “Arrived” and “is sleeping” need nothing after them.

try.q: Label each part of the sentence.
try.why: Fatima (who) · ate (action) · lunch (what she ate).

try.q: Put the words in order to make a sentence.
try.why: Subject, then verb, then object.

try.q: Which group of words is a complete sentence by itself?
try.why: “The shop opens at nine.” has a subject, a verb and a finished idea. “Because it was late.” has a subject (it) and a verb (was), but the idea is unfinished. You’ll practise that in lessons 1.2 and 1.3.

build.prompt: Write **2 sentences** about what you do after class. Use a subject and a verb in each one.

checks.t: Each sentence has a subject (who or what).
Each sentence has a verb (what happens).
At least one sentence has an object.
Each sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with punctuation.

build.sample: I meet my friends at the café. We drink coffee and talk.

spot.intro: A **complete sentence** passes three checks: it says **who or what**, it has a **verb**, and it **finishes the idea**.

examples.note: Complete: all three checks passed.
Not complete: who or what closes?
Not complete: there is no verb.

try.q: Is each group of words a complete sentence?
try.why: Check for a subject, a verb and a finished idea.

try.q: Which is a complete sentence?
try.why: “The bus is late.” has a subject (the bus), a verb (is) and a finished idea.

try.q: What is missing? “Drinks coffee every morning.”
try.why: We don’t know who drinks coffee. Add a subject: “My father drinks coffee every morning.”

try.q: What is missing? “My parents at home.”
try.why: There is no verb. “My parents are at home.”

try.q: Choose the word that completes the sentence: “The students ___ in the library.”
try.why: “The students study in the library.” uses a complete verb.

try.q: Which word completes the sentence? “___ plays football every weekend.”
try.why: A subject names who plays: Ahmed.

try.q: Put the words in order.
try.why: Subject (Our class) + verb (starts) + the rest.

try.q: A complete sentence must…
try.why: Length doesn’t matter. A complete idea does.

build.prompt: Write **3 complete sentences** about your favourite place to eat.
build.placeholder: My favourite place to eat is ...

checks.t: Each sentence says who or what.
Each sentence has a verb.
Each sentence makes sense on its own.
Each sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with punctuation.

build.sample: My favourite restaurant is near my house. The chicken is delicious. I go there every Friday.

spot.intro: A **fragment** looks like a sentence but is missing a **subject**, a **verb**, or the **rest of the idea**. Add what’s missing to fix it.

examples.note: Missing a subject → “We went to the market.”
Missing a verb → “My new phone is very fast.”
Unfinished idea → “We stayed home because it was raining.”

try.q: Sentence or fragment?
try.why: “Walked to the gym” has no subject. “After the lesson ended” leaves the idea unfinished.

try.q: What is missing? “Studies English every night.”
try.why: Who studies? Add a subject: “Rana studies English every night.”

try.q: What is missing? “The big red bus.”
try.why: What did the bus do? “The big red bus stopped.”

try.q: Which choice fixes the fragment “Because the road was closed.”?
options: Because the road was closed, we took another route.
Because the road was closed and.
try.why: The first choice finishes the idea with a main part.

try.q: Fix the fragment by adding a subject.
try.why: Many answers work: any subject + “went to the dentist.”, for example “My sister went to the dentist.”

try.q: Fix the fragment by adding a verb.
try.why: Any verb that makes sense works: “My new laptop is very fast.”

try.q: Put the words in order to make a complete sentence.
answers: Because it was late, we took a taxi.
try.why: The “because” part needs a main part after the comma.

try.q: Which one is NOT a fragment?
try.why: “We met after class.” has a subject and a verb and finishes the idea.

build.prompt: Write **3 complete sentences** about last weekend. Try to start one with **After** or **Because** and finish the idea.

checks.t: Every sentence has a subject and a verb.
My “After…” or “Because…” sentence has a comma and a main part.
I have no fragments.
Each sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with punctuation.

build.sample: On Friday, I visited my grandmother. After we had lunch, we watched a film. I was tired because I slept late.

spot.intro: A **run-on** joins two sentences with **no punctuation**. A **comma splice** joins them with **only a comma**. Fix them with a **full stop**, or a **comma + and / but / so**.

examples.t: The bus was late we walked.
examples.note: Run-on → “The bus was late, so we walked.”

examples.t: It was cold, we wore coats.
examples.note: Comma splice → “It was cold, so we wore coats.”

examples.t: I was hungry. I bought a sandwich.
examples.note: Two separate sentences. Also correct.

try.q: What is wrong with each one?

items.t: My brother works in a bank he starts at eight.
The test was hard, I studied a lot.
The test was hard, but I passed.
We cooked dinner, and then we watched TV.

try.why: Two full sentences need a full stop, or a comma plus a joining word.

try.q: What is wrong? “It rained all day we stayed inside.”
try.why: Two sentences are stuck together without any punctuation.

try.q: What is wrong? “It rained all day, we stayed inside.”
try.why: A comma alone can’t join two sentences.

try.q: Which is the best fix for “I missed the bus, I was late for class.”?
options: I missed the bus, so I was late for class.
I missed the bus, I was late for class.
I missed the bus I was late for class.
I missed the bus, and, I was late for class.
try.why: Comma + so joins the two ideas correctly. A full stop would also work.

try.q: Fix this run-on using a full stop or a joining word.
try.show: Maria likes tea her husband likes coffee.
accept: Maria likes tea. Her husband likes coffee.
Maria likes tea; her husband likes coffee.
patterns: ^(While|Although|Whereas) Maria likes tea, her husband likes coffee\.$
^Maria likes tea, (but|and|while|whereas) her husband likes coffee\.$
try.why: Several fixes work: a full stop (“Maria likes tea. Her husband likes coffee.”), a comma + but / and, or a word like “While”. What matters is that the two ideas are no longer stuck together.

try.q: Fix this comma splice with a comma and and, but or so.
try.show: The café was full, we left.
try.why: “…, so we left.” shows the result. “and” and “but” are also correct joining words here.

try.q: Put the words in order.
answers: I was tired, so I went to bed early.
try.why: Comma + so joins two complete ideas.

try.q: Tap the LAST word of the first sentence.
try.text: The shop closes at nine we need to hurry.
try.why: “The shop closes at nine” is the first sentence. Put a full stop after “nine”.

build.prompt: Write **3 sentences** about a day when something went wrong. Join at least one pair of ideas with a **comma and and / but / so**.

checks.t: Each sentence can stand on its own.
I joined two ideas with a comma and and / but / so.
I have no run-ons or comma splices.
Each sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with punctuation.

build.sample: I woke up late, so I missed the bus. I ran to the station. The next bus came ten minutes later, but I was still late for class.

spot.intro: Use a **capital letter** for the first word, for **I**, and for **names** (people, places, days, months, languages). End with **.** (statement), **?** (question) or **!** (strong feeling).

examples.t: On Monday, Ali and I visit Maple Park.
examples.note: Capitals: On, Monday, Ali, I, Maple Park.
A question ends with ?
Use ! for strong feeling, but not too often.

try.q: Tap every word that needs a capital letter.
try.text: on friday, fatima and i visited maple park.
try.why: Capitals: On, Friday, Fatima, I, Maple Park.

try.q: Which sentence is correct?
try.why: Languages and the first word start with capitals.

try.q: Choose the end punctuation: “Where is the library ___”
try.why: It is a question, so it ends with ?

try.q: Choose the end punctuation: “What a beautiful day ___”
try.why: ! shows strong feeling. A full stop is also acceptable here.

try.q: Fix the capitals and punctuation.
try.show: my sister studies in maple town
accept: My sister studies in Maple Town.
try.why: Capital for the first word and for Maple Town, plus a full stop.

try.q: Fix the capital and punctuation.
try.why: Start with a capital letter and end the question with ?

try.q: Which words need capitals? “we met on saturday at noon”
try.why: The first word and the day of the week.

try.q: Put the words in order.
answers: Does your brother live in Maple Town?
try.why: A question ends with ? and place names have capitals.

build.prompt: Write **3 sentences** about yourself: your name, where you live, and one language you speak.

checks.t: My name and the place I live start with capital letters.
The language I wrote has a capital letter.
Every sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with punctuation.

build.sample: My name is Noor. I live in Maple Town. I speak Arabic and English.

spot.intro: Use a **comma** between items in a **list**, and after an **introductory word or phrase** at the start of a sentence.

examples.t: I bought rice, eggs, and milk.
examples.note: Commas separate the items in a list.

examples.t: After lunch, we went to the gym.
examples.note: A comma follows the introductory phrase.

examples.t: We went to the gym after lunch.
examples.note: No comma when the phrase comes at the end.

try.q: Which is punctuated correctly? “We ordered tea coffee and juice.”
options: We ordered tea, coffee, and juice.
We ordered tea, coffee and juice.
We ordered, tea coffee and juice.
We ordered tea coffee, and juice.
try.why: Both of the first two are fine. The comma before “and” is optional: just stay consistent.

try.q: Tap the word that needs a comma after it.
try.why: “After class” is an introductory phrase, so “After class, we played volleyball.”

try.q: Add the missing comma.
try.why: A comma follows the introductory word “Yesterday”.

try.q: Add the missing commas.
try.show: I packed shoes socks and a towel.
accept: I packed shoes, socks, and a towel.
I packed shoes, socks and a towel.
try.why: Both versions work. Use commas between the items.

try.q: Which sentence is correct?
try.why: The comma goes after the whole introductory phrase “Before work”.

try.q: Does the sentence need a comma?

items.t: Every morning I walk to school.
I walk to school every morning.

try.why: A comma is needed only when the time phrase comes first.

try.q: Why is there a comma in “Finally, we arrived.”?
try.why: A comma follows an introductory word.

try.q: Put the words in order.
try.why: Introductory phrase, comma, then the main sentence.

build.prompt: Write **3 sentences** about your morning. Use **one list** of three things and **one sentence** that starts with a time phrase such as “After breakfast” or “Every morning”.

checks.t: My list has commas between the items.
My time phrase at the start is followed by a comma.
Each sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with punctuation.

build.sample: Every morning, I wake up at six. I eat eggs, bread, and cheese. Then I walk to the bus stop.

spot.intro: English word order is usually **Subject → Verb → Object**. Words like **always, usually, often, sometimes, never** go **before** the main verb, but **after** am / is / are. **Place** usually comes before **time** at the end.

examples.t: Khaled reads the news every day.
examples.note: Subject, verb, object, then time.

examples.t: I always drink tea.  ·  She is often late.
examples.note: Before the main verb, but after “is”.

examples.t: We met at the café on Friday.
examples.note: Place first, then time.

try.q: Put the words in order.
answers: Khaled reads the news every day.
try.why: Subject, verb, object, then the time.

try.q: Which sentence is in the correct order?
options: My sister plays tennis on Saturdays.
Plays my sister tennis on Saturdays.
My sister tennis plays on Saturdays.
My sister plays on Saturdays tennis.
try.why: Subject (My sister) + verb (plays) + object (tennis).

try.q: Put the words in order.
answers: I always drink tea in the morning.
try.why: “Always” goes before the main verb.

try.q: Which sentence is correct?
try.why: After “is”, the frequency word follows: “is never”.

try.q: Put the words in order.
answers: We met at the café on Friday.
try.why: Place (at the café) comes before time (on Friday).

try.q: Put the words in the correct order.
try.why: Subject (My uncle) + verb (drives) + object (a taxi).

try.q: Which sentences are in correct order? (more than one can be right)
try.why: “Often” can go before the verb or at the end, but not between the verb and its object.

try.q: Put the words in order.
try.why: After “are”, the frequency word comes next.

build.prompt: Write **3 sentences** about your week. Use **one frequency word** (always, usually, often, sometimes, never) and put a **place or time at the end** of one sentence.

checks.t: My frequency word is before the main verb (or after am / is / are).
One sentence ends with a place or a time.
Each sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with punctuation.

build.sample: I usually study in the library. My brother often plays football after school. We never eat dinner late.

spot.intro: A **statement** gives information. A **yes/no question** starts with **Do / Does / Is / Are**. A **Wh- question** starts with **Where / What / When / Why / How**, then **do / does / is / are**, then the subject. After **does**, the verb has **no -s**.

examples.t: You live in Maple Town.  →  Do you live in Maple Town?
examples.note: Add do at the start.
Question word + do + subject + verb.
After “does”, the verb stays simple: study.

try.q: Which is a correct question?
try.why: Does + subject + base verb (work).

try.q: Put the words in order to make a question.
try.why: Question word + do + subject + verb.

try.q: Turn the statement into a question.
try.why: With “is”, swap the subject and the verb: “Is she a nurse?”

try.q: Turn the statement into a question.
try.why: Start with “Do” and keep the verb simple.

try.q: Choose the word: “___ he play football on Fridays?”
try.why: He → does.

try.q: Choose the word: “What ___ your brother study?”
try.why: Your brother (he) → does.

try.q: Put the words in order.
try.why: Is + subject + the rest.

try.q: Statement or question?

items.t: How do you get to campus?

try.why: Questions start with do / does / is / are or a question word.

build.prompt: Write **2 questions** you would ask a new classmate and **1 statement** about yourself.

checks.t: I wrote one yes/no question (Do / Does / Is / Are).
I wrote one question with a question word.
My questions end with a question mark.
Each sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with punctuation.

build.sample: Where do you live? Do you like football? I live near the university.

spot.intro: This is the **Stage 1 review**: ten mixed questions from every lesson. Pass with **8 out of 10** to mark any lessons you skipped as done.

build.prompt: Write **4 sentences** about a place you like. Include **one list**, **one question**, and **one sentence that starts with a time phrase**.

checks.t: Every sentence is complete (subject, verb, finished idea).
I have no run-ons or comma splices.
My list and my time phrase have the right commas.
Capital letters and end punctuation are correct.

build.sample: My favourite place is the beach near my house. In the evening, the air is cool. I bring a towel, a book, and a snack. Do you like the beach too?

subject.label: Finding the subject
subject.good: You can find the subject, the who or what.
subject.improve: Ask “who or what does the action?” to find the subject.

verb.label: Finding the verb
verb.improve: The verb is the action (or is / are). Find it first.

object.label: Objects
object.good: You can tell when a sentence has an object.
object.improve: Ask “who or what?” after the verb to find an object. Some sentences don’t have one.

complete.label: Complete sentences
complete.improve: Check for a subject, a verb and a finished idea.

fragment.label: Fixing fragments
fragment.improve: A fragment is missing a subject, a verb, or part of the idea. Add the missing piece.

runon.label: Run-ons
runon.improve: Two sentences need a full stop, or a comma + and / but / so.

splice.label: Comma splices
splice.improve: A comma alone can’t join two sentences. Add and / but / so, or use a full stop.

caps.label: Capital letters
caps.improve: Capitalize the first word, I, names, days, months and languages.

punct.label: End punctuation
punct.good: You choose the right end punctuation.
punct.improve: Use . for statements and ? for questions.

comma.label: Basic commas
comma.improve: Use commas in lists and after an introductory word or phrase.

order.label: Word order
order.improve: Use Subject + Verb + Object. Put place before time.

question.label: Questions
question.improve: Use do / does / is / are first, and keep the verb simple after does.
